utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please -- wait, wait, wait. All right. You can call the case now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen, Your Honours. I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning -- good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I am -- and also good afternoon to my learned friends of the Defence. I'm here together with Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio and our case manager, Mrs. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you and your staff. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to the learned friends from the OTP. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones I appear for Mr. Oric. We have with us our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam, and good afternoon to you, too, and your team. So an announcement, first of all. Tomorrow you know we've shifted the sitting from the afternoon to the morning, but we will not be starting at 9.00 because a Status Conference in the Seselj case that had been scheduled for after the Oric case being -- the accused has asked, for personal reasons that I feel are justified, to have the Status Conference first thing in the morning. So we will have the -- rather, not you. I will have the Status Conference in Seselj at 8.30 in the morning, hopefully to finish by 9.30, and then we'll start with your case at 10.00 in the morning, all right? And then we'll go right through until quarter to 2.00, as scheduled. All right. I have some information on the exchange that has been going on between the two parties on the Prosecution rebuttal case. I take it that you will be filing the proper instrument tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we'll deal with that matter afterwards, unless you have got some submissions to make now. Okay. So that will come later. Mr. Wubben, you had promised us to come, as we had indicated to you that we would be quite willing to hear what you have to say on our plans to appoint a handwriting expert. Do you have any submissions which you would like us to take into consideration but which will of course be of no binding value, please go ahead, and try to keep them as short as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have several issues to convey to the Court. Indeed, it is an advising to start with the issue of who to be appointed as an expert by the Trial Chamber. Well, any such appointment of a Court expert is fully to the discretion of the Trial Chamber. I advise that there is no compelling reason that such an expert should be familiar with Cyrillic as well as Latin, in special when it relates to signatures where the same elements in same order matters, even illegible, and that's contrary to Cyrillic handwriting. So far this condition of being familiar with Cyrillic language has not been an issue with the Defence in order to contest any evidence. Also, membership of a shared professional association should not prevent such a nomination. Whenever a Trial Chamber expert is not shown the outcome in detail of the file to expert report, this should not be a problem at all. The e-mail from the German expert shown in court last Thursday by the Defence counsel does not change my point of view. The text of the paragraph in the e-mail involved should be read as a whole and not by -- only by highlighting selected part of it. In that e-mail there is no suggestion that experts during their examination are influenced by opinions from colleagues within that association. Rather, it is in expectation that there are consistent conclusions in proficiency tests, collaborative exercises or co-working in real cases on the same material, due to the many efforts to bring them into line -- to bring into line the allocation and examination methodology of the handwriting experts. Even if Trial Chamber would prefer two experts, then these persons might arrive from nationality [sic]. It's the expertise in examination that should be neutral. In that respect, the Trial Chamber is free to seek a qualified expert. The second issue, Your Honours, is the issue whether the Trial Chamber expert is to be considered more credible on forehand. Well, in the same field, the expert or experts, once nominated by the Trial Chamber, should not be viewed as being more credible simply because of an appointment by this Chamber. Also, the experts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to address the Trial Chamber on this. I mean, we've made it clear. The fact that we appoint him or her does not mean that we consider him or her better than yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I shall go -- move to the third issue of producing a report by the expert nominated by the Trial Chamber. Prior to his testimony, the Trial Chamber expert should produce a report, in my opinion, even given the possibility of consulting by parties of another expert on behalf of cross-examination or examination. Within the adversarial system, it should be possible to prepare adequately for examination or cross-examination based upon a priorly disclosed report and also in order to challenge the conclusions of that report in whole or in part. Rule 94 bis applies mutatis mutandis, meaning that the report will be in evidence as well as the testimony in court by the Trial Chamber expert. And subsequently, as it finds last Wednesday by the Presiding Judge, if parties want to bring their expert over to give evidence again, then there should be a possibility to recall their expert later on. In the report, the Trial Chamber expert should make use of international accepted standards or scales of probability and possibility are referred to a similar approach of the standard as provided in the annex of the expert report of the -- by the Prosecution regarding the applicable scale. The next issue is the reference material available to the Trial Chamber expert from the reports of parties' experts. In my opinion, the expert nominated by the Trial Chamber should be provided by the questioned, so-called Q documents, and the known-signature documents, it has the reference material also known as the K documents used by the expert of the Prosecution in 2004 and related to the accused. These Q documents and K documents had been partly used by the expert from Defence, meaning that the Trial Chamber expert should focus on examination of signatures related to the accused. No more material is advised. The Trial Chamber expert will thus have the availability of the originals or if copies have been examined, the copies used, and subsequently exercise the examination requested by the Trial Chamber. So there is also no need to provide the Trial Chamber expert with the expert reports from parties. The identifying of the group of the so-called K documents. As stated before, the so-called K documents are documents with the known signatures from accused. These K documents used by Prosecution expert in his report are already all in evidence, not only the aid referred to by the Defence expert, but also the other ones up to K35 are in evidence. Contrary to the so-called non-contentious documents in the expert report from Defence, again apart from P100, those are the eight K documents. It is not contested by parties that the signatures on the K documents are from the hands of the accused. It is not fair to say, as the Defence counsel did last Wednesday, when he referred to P100 as a collection of signatures allegedly made by his client during the course of his interview. After all, the Prosecution has evidence that the signatures have been placed by the accused. The placing of those signatures have been confirmed in the two declarations from the OTP investigators, Tedder and Kelly. These two affidavits have been accepted by the Defence and ever since never been contested. Moreover, the Defence -- I apologise. The Defence had put it to the expert, Doctorandus Fagel of the Prosecution during his cross-examination in October 2004 that Naser Oric provided them, those reference signatures, willingly. That's why the expert could use them. The following issue is the samples of signatures to be available for the examination by the Trial Chamber expert. When it comes to the contested signatures examined by both experts with contrasting conclusions in the field of alleged signatures from accused, I counted ten questioned documents examined by both parties' experts. I refer also in addition to the number mentioned last week, P13, Your Honour. So in total, ten documents within that contrasting conclusion by both parties' experts. In addition, the expert by the Defence examined also three documents, Prosecution Exhibits mentioned under paragraph 4 of his report. Those are exhibits P176, P213, and P330. The Prosecution is happy to provide as well these last three Prosecution exhibits to the Trial Chamber expert. I will leave that decision to the discretion of Your Honours. The expert nominated by the Trial Chamber should examine these 13 documents, including ten contrasting conclusions by the experts, and compare the signatures with the known signatures of the accused, that is to say, these so-called K documents as mentioned in the expert report filed by the Prosecution. So to compare the signatures included in the number of 32 Q documents with the signature in a total number of 35 K documents as in especially the report of the expert from the Prosecution. In the report by the Defence expert, there are also other documents alleged to be non-contentious signatures. These so-called N documents are referring to signatures of Hamed Salihovic, N documents refer to Naser Oric, and N documents referring to Hamdija Fejzic. In my opinion, these N documents referred to in the expert report of Bilic should not be subject to a subsequent examination by the Trial Chamber expert. I underline that in our response to the Defence motion, filing the expert report under Rule 94 bis, the Prosecution did not accept the expert statement of Mr. Bilic under 94 bis. And the Prosecution accordingly contest that these so-called non-contentious document bear a known signature of the alleged originator, as there is no evidence for that, apart from the eight K documents used by the expert of the Defence. Therefore, I advise the Court to exclude from examination by Trial Chamber expert, firstly, the alleged non-contentious documents, handwritings, and signatures related to Hamed Salihovic; secondly, the non-contentious documents related to the accused, except of course the eight K documents under N5 to N12; and thirdly, the non-contentious documents related to Hamdija Fejzic. There is no evidence provided that these alleged non-contentious documents include non-signatures or signature witness person to be placed by alleged three originators. They are simply saying no control copies available. The alleged non-contentious documents, apart from, again, the eight K documents, haven't even been disclosed or filed by the Defence. Here the safe-guards of Rule 94 bis applies. As there are no valid control copies, one should assume that the documents will not be agreed upon by parties as being non-contentious. My conclusion is that the Trial Chamber expert will examine the signatures alleged to be from Naser Oric and then compare these signatures from those mentioned 32 questioned documents and additional three contentious documents under P176, P230, and P330, with the signatures from the mentioned 35 K documents. The other material related to other two persons should not be subject to that examination by the Trial Chamber expert. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Mr. Wubben. Mr. Jones or Madam Vidovic. I don't know whose -- I suppose it's Mr. Jones on this. Do you have any remarks?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We don't propose to provide a detailed reply to the remarks made just now by Mr. Wubben. Really, I maintain the submissions which I made last Wednesday, which were made really in the spirit of assisting the Trial Chamber in exercising its discretion and not an attempt to interfere with that discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was the idea of inviting you or accepting your suggestion to accept -- to hear submissions from you because we are not necessarily any wiser, but it's always wise to hear submissions because, as always, something to learn from that. So -- and I think we have heard some submissions which we'll definitely take into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And it was a fairly lengthy submission, so it's possible in the next day or two that we come back on one point or another, having considered it, but at the moment we have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, I just wanted to confirm to you that we have moved -- continue moving on this and we should be able to conclude on this matter pretty soon. There's one final matter that I would like to ask you to do some brain-storming about, and this is how it -- this might affect the final briefs, because obviously some -- I'm not saying that all, of course, but some very significant submissions may be affected, depending on what the findings will be ultimately and what the position will be. At the present moment, my suggestion is that since you are expected to be working on the preparation of your final briefs in any case while this exercise is going on, you keep in mind the following: That there are two conflicting or almost conflicting submissions to the Trial Chamber with regard to some of these documents, particularly the ten. And I would suggest that you keep that at the back of your mind. As you yourself said, the fact that we are going to appoint an expert of our own does not necessarily mean that we are going definitely to have a final, clear picture of where this matter should go, either one side or the other. I, for one, do not know what to expect and we could have any kind of report. So please keep all options open while you continue preparing your final -- your final briefs. And then of course you will make the adjustments that are required as we go -- as we go along. I also wish to confirm to you that when we have the report of our expert, it's certainly not our intention to cut you off and deny you the possibility of either examining or cross-examining the expert or even recalling your own experts in due course. There is the other alternative I mentioned before, that the fact that even your experts are independent experts does not, in our opinion, constitute an obstacle in you having them present, sitting next to you, while you are examining or cross-examining our expert. Probably that will prove more economic timewise, and it would spare us having to go through the whole process of recalling witnesses and therefore delaying the procedures. But I would invite you to be open-minded in this recommendation because we could end up being the most surprised of all when we have this report come from our expert. It has happened before, and I do not exclude anything. So I thank you so much on behalf of my two colleagues and on my own behalf for having been very constructive in your recommendations and suggestions and submissions to the Trial Chamber on this matter. As I said, some of your submissions have been, indeed, very informative and very enlightening, and I'm pretty sure that some of them will be taken into consideration. We will, of course, inform you in due course of what our decision is. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, have you given any thought to the general schedule that would follow from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have -- MR. DI FAZIO: From this -- what I'm wondering about is the four-week period going to start at some earlier point or after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, of course we have, and of course we know that if we give one document to the expert to examine rather than 50, he's going to finish his -- there is the other option of him coming over or her coming over to present -- make an oral presentation of the report and then you give you the opportunity to re-call your experts. That has a handicap because you will be taken by surprise more or less as much as we will if the expert comes over and presents -- makes an oral presentation of his findings. So having had second and third thoughts about this, although we haven't discussed -- finalised the discussions on this particular issue, my colleagues and I, I will be suggesting that we will have a written report rather than an oral presentation because that will give us -- put us all in the condition of knowing beforehand what the witness could be asked, putting us on notice on what questions one could ask to the witness and giving you also time to consult with your experts on what questions to put and so on and so forth. I think I'm making myself clear. On the basis of this depends the rest of the schedule. I have got various options that we have been working up on with our staff. I think we have to leave options open. Priority being given to two consideration: To lose as much -- as least time as possible; that's number one. At the same time, secure to both parties all the due process rights that you have to deal with this matter as thoroughly as possible because as you yourself understand and submit, these issues are of fundamental importance to this trial, the authenticity of certain documents. So we don't intend by any stretch of imagination to belittle the importance of this exercise, and we will be giving you all the opportunity. When I say you will be in the meantime preparing for your final brief, reason is very obvious and a very simple one. The final brief does not depend entirely, or to a large extent, on the authenticity of these ten documents, 15, 20, 30. Of course if they are authentic, it does have a bearing. If they are not authentic, or the prevalence of -- the indication is that they are not authentic, then of course the whole scenario changes as well, as far as certain issues are concerned. As far as certain other issues, I think you can continue to prepare and have your pre-trial -- not pre-trial, your final brief in place, ready to be baked. There is no reason why you should delay on preparing your final brief simply because we are going to deal with this exercise and you don't know what the outcome is going to be, just as much as we don't know what the outcome is going to be. We will be making our own preparations as well. Of course -- and ultimately we will depend on your final submissions in regard. All right? But there may well need to be shifting of the dates that we had proposed as a consequence, but we are still hoping to be able to conclude -- once we have an indication from the expert that we will appoint as to how long he or she would require, then of course we can plan better. The thing is that this exercise will start while we are still not yet finished the evidentiary stage, and the evidentiary stage, I mean also rebuttal and rejoinder, if there will be a rebuttal and rejoinder, obviously. Because if there won't be, then obviously we're talking of one starting immediately after. All right? Yes, if you have any queries on -- in this context, on this regard, please let us know. Please rest -- put your mind at rest that we will give you all the opportunities that -- all the opportunities that you need to prepare yourself well. All right? Madam Vidovic, Mr. Jones, any comments? Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I thank you so much for your understanding and your cooperation. Madam Usher will now -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Professor Bilic, and welcome back. The time has arrived to start with your expert testimony. The Rules of this Tribunal require that before you start giving evidence you make a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony you will testify the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is contained in a piece of paper that Madam Usher is going to hand to you. Please read it out and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Professor. Please make yourself comfortable. Now, you're a professional man and I'm going to leave you straight in the hands of Mr. Jones, I take it, who will be examining you in chief in relation to your expert report. Mr. Jones. He will then be followed by Mr. Wubben, who will cross-examine you. We expect you to be here till -- hopefully Thursday, and we'll try to wind up your testimony on Thursday, which would make it possible for you to return to your homeland or to your residence in -- before the weekend. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Jones:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor Bilic. If you could please give the Court your full name.

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Esad Bilic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And confirm, if you would, the following details. You were born on the 18th of August, 1948, in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You graduated from the University of Sarajevo, completed post-graduate study, and you are now a professor in education and psychology?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By profession, you're an expert in the scientific examination of documents, and you've been working in that field for 30 years?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is it correct that you started your career as a police expert, examining documents for the Ministry of the Interior in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive training for your work with the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you receive that training?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: I received that training -- or rather, the traineeship in the centres of the former Yugoslavia, Ljubljana, Zagreb, Belgrade, and Skopje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you receive training from mentors in the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're now a sworn court expert in the federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Brcko district. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: In Brcko district, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're also a member of a society of court experts of Republika Srpska and you've worked in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you also acted as a mentor to police experts in Bosnia and Herzegovina, instructing them in the methods and techniques of document examination?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you have your own laboratory for document examination?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, do you currently have an officially registered agency for graphology and an agency for investigating counterfeit money, which you yourself established?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you engaged by the central bank in Bosnia and Herzegovina as an expert?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're currently a member of the association of court experts of the federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and before the war you were a member of the commission for forensic document examination. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, to be a member of the commission for forensic examination of documents before the war, did you have to pass an official state examination as an expert?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you regularly attend meetings with colleagues to harmonise your work and methods?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you published in this field and your publications being those listed in your curriculum vitae?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many examinations of handwriting can you estimate that you've done in total during your career?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Several -- several tens of thousands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you still regularly do handwriting analysis?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you testify regularly in court in Bosnia as a court-appointed expert on a cantonal, municipal, and state level?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you about to publish a book on the forensic identification of handwriting and signatures?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before coming to the report which you prepared in this case, I want you to explain for us a little your analytical methodology, and if you could tell us, please, what are the phases, broadly speaking, of investigation when you're asked to compare contentious and non-contentious writing or signature samples?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will try to explain the process roughly. There is the preliminary phase, which consists in the analytical examination of contentious documents or signatures or documents containing contentious text. Then there follows an examination of non-contentious reference documents. After this critical examination, there follows the process of collecting adequate contentious and non-contentious documents. Contentious documents may prove to be inadequate for examination for several reasons, which is why it may be necessary to seek adequate documentation, mainly originals. Photocopies need to be avoided. The person commissioning the examination needs to prepare a solid and appropriate sample of a non-contentious document, whilst respecting the principles dictated by the methodology of document examination. This is the crucial and most difficult stage. A well-prepared sample of non-contentious documents will most certainly yield objective results, that's to say, findings --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I stop you there for a moment. Sorry to interrupt, and we'll move on to the next phase in a moment.

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But is it right then to say that you take a critical approach to the samples that you're provided with in that you assess whether they're sufficient in terms of quantity and quality even before starting?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: That's of fundamental importance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, do all forensic document examiners take that critical approach?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: It depends. Most -- all of them should take such an approach. I will proceed to explain what course the examination takes. When both contentious and non-contentious documents have been obtained, the first stage of examination needs to be applied, which consists of visual and instrumental examination of a given signature or a handwritten note or whatever is contained in a given document. The document taken as a whole cannot be looked at in its individual parts; it has to be looked as a whole. If you look at the document, you cannot merely look at the hand -- at the signature but, rather, at the whole document. So first of all, the documents need to be looked at individually, with special reference to what is contentious in the document. It is in this way that all the documents need to be examined and all the particular aspects can -- of a given document, discrepancies that pertain either to the contents or to the stamp impression or the typewriter used and so on and so forth, all of these discrepancies have to be examined. And once this is done, photographs are taken of a given document, a scanner is used or a camera. What then follows is the presentation of the non-contentious sample. There has to be a special examination for every single aspect that is trying to be analysed against the non-contentious documents. Once this particular analysis is finished, when the documentation is made, everything has been photographed or scanned, the next stage follows, which is that of comparing the similarities or dissimilarities in the documents, which is of crucial importance. At that point, the examiner needs to assess, evaluate, and analyse the similarities and dissimilarities in which of these prevail. Based on that, the findings will be drafted. The comparison can be done in several directions, again based on visual or instrumental examination, depending on what the target of the examination is. It can be done in several ways, several aspects. If more writers are involved, we have to compare the authentic, genuine, known handwriting with that which is contentious. This is a very complex and time-consuming task. It is far from the comparisons we have in geometry, for instance, whether you compare a square with a square; this is a completely different process. Once the comparisons have been drawn and all the different variations existing in the handwriting stamps, typewritten texts, and so on and so forth have been found, photographic enlargements are then produced which will form the basis of the examination; that's to say folders are created containing these enlargements which will be instrumental in enabling the persons who will look at them to understand what they illustrate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll stop you is there. Sorry. Sorry to interrupt. That's a very helpful explanation you've been giving. Just to apply some of this to your report in this case. Did you indeed prepare some of these maps for this case, and are they an illustration of your conclusions or are they are complete -- a complete explanation of those conclusions?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. That was something I had to produce because this was a highly complex task requiring very clear and to-the-point findings. That is why I produced these maps containing my findings that followed logically the course of my examination. They can be analysed and assessed. That's why they have been created.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And may I just -- one clarification. Are these maps an illustration of your analysis or do they summarise all of the results of your analysis?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: This is only part of what was analysed. It is really impossible to produce maps containing all these because they would take far too much space. I believe that what has been presented here will be sufficient. They were designed to help the observer, the beholder, to follow logically the sequence of contested documents, non-contested document, different fragments of these, so that even a person who is not familiar with these documents, to grasp and analyse for himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then following these phases you've described, do you then draft your analysis and your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. I critically re-test all the findings that I have arrived at, that is to say, I critically re-examine the findings I have made. Sometimes a person gets carried away, overvalues or undervalues certain items, and this can only show to have happened after some time has elapsed. That is why in order to reach objective and high-quality findings, one has to re-examine the findings. It is only at the end of this that conclusions are formed which are then structured along a scale of probability, of possibility. And again, this methodology will depend on the examiner who is involved and on the experience he has.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the analysis you do, are you sometimes able to reach a firm or definite conclusion and not just a probabilistic one?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: The aim of any forensic analysis is to provide a finding which will be as conclusive as possible, because any other conclusion which is a probabilistic one is of no assistance to the Court. That is why we have the different categories of possibly yes, possibly not, high possibility, high probability, and so on and so forth. The conclusiveness of the findings will depend on the quality of the samples which are being examined. That's why I said that the sample itself will determine 90 per cent of the examination and the findings that will be reached. Whenever it is possible to say something with absolute certainty, then one should do so, of course if the samples provided permit that sort of conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And what do you do if you don't have the means to reach a firm conclusion but you're asked to give a conclusion nonetheless? Is that when you would use a probabilistic conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: If it is impossible to reach any conclusive findings, then of course we will have to draw upon these inconclusive levels of findings. It will again depend on contentious document. It will depend on the critical approach of the examiner. However, I myself reach such inconclusive findings most often when I examine photocopies when the corresponding originals cannot be found. In such cases, I'd rather not give any findings at all; however, sometimes it might prove necessary to do so. Photocopies can be highly deceitful and misleading. They may mislead; that's why it's best not to give any sort of conclusions in relation to photocopies. Again, when one is deciding about the finding, it will depend on the quality of the reproduction of a photocopy and on a number of other aspects that will shape one's conclusion. And it will then -- this will be decisive for whether the conclusion will be on top of the probability scale or at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Well, if at the moment you could be shown --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The witness could be shown his report. We have a revised English translation, and I'd like to express my appreciation to CLSS who very diligently reviewed the report beforehand and helpfully pointed out some revisions, so we have a revised English version which is available for everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also wish to thank CLSS on behalf of the Tribunal because this proved to be very useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, first of all, while that's being distributed, Professor Bilic, if you could look at what's been put in front of you and tell us whether you recognise that as the report you produced in this case.

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the report I submitted for this case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to come to this report in detail, but for the moment I would just like you to refer to pages 22, 29, and 34. And I should say the page references are the same for the Bosnian and English, which is helpful. So on those pages do we see some of the general and specific characteristics of handwriting that you analyse?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the pages you've referred to, I mentioned only the most obvious discrepancies which were listed here. And immediately following these particular pages, maps can be found where you can see --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as I say, Professor Bilic, we're going to come to the conclusions in a moment, and in fact I'm still looking at general questions. It was really to draw attention to these characteristics of handwriting, formation of small and large graphemes, inclining writing angle, calibration. These are a number of the things which you look at when you analyse handwriting. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I say, we're going to come to your report in detail in a moment, but I still have one or two general questions. In referring to samples you've referred to the importance of the quantity and quality of the samples. Now, quantity, I imagine, is self-explanatory. You need sufficient numbers of documents to analyse. But for quality, can you explain a little bit what factors are relevant to the quality of the sample to be analysed.

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: I will give you a direct answer. The non-contentious document has to have sufficient quantities, of course; that's first. As for the quality, it has to do with the following categories: The way the non-contentious documents came into being. They must have come into being outside of the contentious documents; however, they should have come into being in that same year, or the same month, but the year is sufficient. Secondly, they should be in their original form rather than photocopies. They should contain writings which were made in the same writing implements as the non-contentious -- as the contentious documents, that's to say, in ball-point pen or in pencil and so on and so forth. Furthermore, there has to be proof of the fact that the non-contentious document was, in fact, produced by the writer concerned. How can we prove this? Well, this can be proved in the case of official documents, for instance. The quality of the documents has to be satisfactory. They have to be made on paper which is of more or less the same quality and so on and so forth. This is, I believe, enough. Everybody understands what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would it be correct, then, that if you have all of the non-contentious samples being written or signed on the same day, is that a good sample or not for analysis?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: That would be a modest sample. That would not suffice for analysis. That would be a so-called situation sample which was made on one day or only in one year and, as such, would not be sufficient for findings, especially when one deals with signatures and the types of documents I examined here. The signatures have to date from a continuous sequence in time, as I myself asked for, in fact. We had cases where we -- writers are deceased, so we had to fall back on the documents dating back in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, perhaps just one final preliminary matter. In your opinion, to analyse handwriting and signatures, do you have to know or do you not the language, grammar, the characters, and the scripts in which the samples are written?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's understood. As an expert, I cannot do an expert analysis of handwritings in Turkish, Arabic, Hebrew, Japanese, or Chinese, for example. I cannot analyse handwriting that uses a different spelling. In the Bosnian language, for example, we have a principle that one letter represents one sound. In other languages, such as English or Dutch, one sound can be represented by two graphemes, that is two letters. The researcher has to be familiar with this. He has to be able to read and write the language and to use it. That can have a significant influence, especially as in Bosnia and Herzegovina two kinds of scripts are used, cursive and block writing are both used. And both scripts are used. Anyone residing in Bosnia and Herzegovina can use both scripts. Some people write in Cyrillic and sign their names in Latin or vice versa. There are reasons for all this which we need not go into now, but one must know all these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, and can I ask: Is there much difference between the Cyrillic and Latin script?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry to interrupt. It's not referring to this recent question, it's about the prior question. Mr. Bilic gave an answer regarding the handwriting. I would like to invite him also to answer also the part of the question by my learned friend regarding the signatures. So does an analyst need to know the language when it refers to signatures only?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'm happy for the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Wubben. Yes. Thank you, Mr. Jones. I'm sure you would agree that it needs to be addressed as in the context that it was put.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know if you understood the question, Professor Bilic. But if you're only analysing the signatures and not the handwriting, is it still necessary to be familiar with the Latin and Cyrillic scripts or the language of the writer?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, I'll answer the question, but we have to clarify something. If a person is to sign his name, he first has to learn to write. The handwriting comes prior to the signature. The signature is very personal. It's idiosyncratic. The signature is never identical to the handwriting and vice versa. But we do have to take into account that for a person to have a signature he has to have a certain handwriting first, whether Cyrillic or Latin. And then according to his personal views and character, a person develops his own signature. The first signature is simply the use of his handwriting to write his name. And then through constant use it becomes idealised and may become so symbolic that individual characters cannot be recognised and one can say what name is written there. Sometimes, of course, we can because it all depends on how frequently the writer has used the signature. Sometimes he simplifies it to such an extent that it's only a curve a line, but it's his line or curve. So in response to Mr. Wubben's question, that is the relationship. A person has to know a script and have a handwriting in a script in order to write. In the former Yugoslavia, both scripts were used and people had to learn to write both.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in brief, is the answer that: Yes, in fact, to analyse a signature --

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, just a few more questions on Cyrillic. Is it, in fact, a different alphabet, would you say, even from the Latin alphabet?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Completely different. The Latin alphabet is a cursive alphabet. It can be sloping or vertical; that's the block manner of writing. The Latin script uses diacritics on the grapheme on letters such as "ch" or "sh" or "j" or "nj," whereas in Cyrillic, in the cursive style of writing, there are no diacritics, only lines. A line is put across the "ch," and this is again something one has to know about in order to understand the explanation. However, those kinds of markings are lacking in Cyrillic. The placing of diacritics is highly unconscious. Also, there is the grapheme, M for example, which illustrates the number of strokes that has to be used. So in Cyrillic every grapheme has more strokes than the corresponding Latin. So this leaves the impression of a more dense kind of writing. If I were to write my own last name in Latin and then in Cyrillic, the signature would be completely different. I think I've clarified sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That's perfectly clear. And in fact just to anticipate one matter, is it correct that Naser Oric signs his name is Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to now go back to your report and look at it in detail. First of all, I think you verified that it's your signature on page 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I believe we'll be taking the break at quarter to 4.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, in 11 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, if you feel that you need a break earlier, if you're uncomfortable, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Any time, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you need a break --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I believe your signature is on page 36, and the date of the report is the 2nd of December, 2005. On page 1 of your report your engagement by the Defence of the Tribunal's order dated 12th October 2006 [sic] is set out. That is the order pursuant to which you received the documents to do the analysis.

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said you worked on the documents from the 26th of October, 2005, when you received them until the 23rd of November, 2005. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One question about the time it takes for this sort of analysis. Could you have conducted your analysis in this case in any less time than that, say, if you'd had two weeks or three weeks?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you explain why it takes a long time to analyse these documents?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: There was a large number of documents. The documents were very complex. I'm referring to the contentious documents. However, the non-contentious documents also had to be prepared. Two of the writers are deceased, which made the work more difficult. Furthermore, the questions put by the Defence were very precise; there were many of them. And I had to do a lot of work. I had to leave everything else to one side and work only on these documents. I had to investigate the signatures and the handwriting. And whether we like it or not, I had to look at the whole document, especially the original documents which required much investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, it's a matter of further clarification. Two of the writers have been deceased. Can my learned friend ask for the names?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to come back to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct that two of the writers are deceased? And remember it's -- we're talking about Naser Oric, Hamdija Fejzic, and Hamed Salihovic. Is it one or two who you say are deceased?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: One. I apologise. I misspoke. Only one is deceased.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which is that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Hamed Salihovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Now, going back to your report, you returned the documents to the Tribunal on the 23rd of November, 2005. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the questioned signatures and handwriting, are those set out on pages 2 to 3 at I to IV, the contentious material?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the non-contentious handwriting and signatures are Hamed Salihovic, Hamdija Fejzic, and Naser Oric. Are those set out on pages 3 to 5 of your report? .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to make a submission, but outside the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think as far as Professor Bilic is concerned, we can start the break now, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Madam Usher will escort you, Professor Bilic. We'll have a 30-minute break. For you it's going to be 35 minutes or a bit less, and we'll have the submission from Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, my learned friend used two labels, the qualifications of signatures, handwriting. It comes to the label of questions and non-contentious handwriting and signatures. I refer to the transcript page 30, lines 6 and line 9. Now we are dealing with the report itself, and it is important to know what we should understand, what should be included, in such a qualification. When it comes to questioned signatures and handwriting, there's a qualification I used myself also, as well as our expert from - yes - from the so-called the Q documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I'm fine with that, and these are -- of course this is contentious material. When it comes to non-contentious handwriting and signatures, I already took the floor in the beginning of this afternoon to underline that the eight K documents is -- are supposed to bear the signature of the accused. These are the known signatures. For the rest of the so-called non-contentious documents in this report, I don't know where the qualification comes from, but we have no knowledge of evidence that these documents bear the signatures and handwriting of the alleged originator. And so my submission is that whenever there is an absence of such evidence and when it is contested by a party, at least the qualification of non-contentious documents being non-contentious by the parties, is not justified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or at least you don't agree with the way it's being put by the Defence. Let me try and see if I have understood you well. There are eight documents which the Defence and -- the Defence expert referred to as the non-contentious, which include an alleged signature by Naser Oric. And your contention is -- or your submission is: Does that mean to say that it is not being contested that that is Naser Oric's signature? Because if it's not contested, then it can be called non-contentious. If it's contested, then it cannot be qualified as non-contentious. As regards the other signatures by Salihovic and Fejzic, alleged signatures, your contention is that there is no way in which you can agree that these are not being contested by the Prosecution. Main reason being that there is nothing on the basis of which one could come to the conclusion that they are by that -- by those two persons?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do I read you well?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So -- and if you wish to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And I want to point out that in the case -- in the group of so-called alleged non-contentious documents referred to Naser Oric, there is a group that's also new without any such evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So the position is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, may I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Please. I mean, it's -- yes, all right. Judge Eser would like to intervene before we give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, because I'm not clear now what you are talking about when you're talking about non-contentious documents with regard to Naser Oric. Do you refer to page 4 and 1, 2, and 5 or what do you mean with non-contentious, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, non-contentious documents are referred to, as I see it, under paragraph 2 of page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: One --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Number N1 up to N12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. The last sentence in N5 and then in the same line up to N12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Yeah. Not N8 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. Eight is with regards to the total number inclusive of Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But you are talking about Oric --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but this is just Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: This is just Oric, Your Honour. Now if you take only the number N5 to N12, these are eight so-called K documents, known signatures, and that's why there is an ERN number in it and one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One, for example, has Hamdija Fejzic and also Naser Oric. All right. So it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: As well as the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In my mind it's clear what the substance of his objection is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour -- well, may I -- I have to say this is really unnecessarily muddying the waters, particularly on a subject where we should try and keep matters clear and not introduce confusion. Mr. Wubben started -- or said that he doesn't know where these terms come from, contentious and non-contentious. Well, they're in his report; they are in this expert's report. That's where they come from. I'm asking him about his report. And the report is very clear in having I to V as contentious, and non-contentious are listed on pages 3 to 5. It couldn't be any clearer. And in fact, we even have an N beforehand to indicate that it's non-contentious. Now, either Mr. Wubben is making a submission which he could just as well make at the end of the trial to say, well, the expert's report can't be accredited because we're not actually sure that N really is non-contentious or that S really is contentious, or whatever. That's up to him. He can make that submission in due course. It's not a matter for objecting to my examination-in-chief. Or in cross-examination he can say to Professor Bilic: How do you actually know that this is non-contentious? The fact is it's a question of methodology. An expert has non-contentious samples and contentious samples and he compares them. That's what he does. And if Mr. Wubben is trying to create a situation where I'm not even able to use those terms --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When the expert has used them himself --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And, Your Honour, it may be a question of terminology. I'm going to use the term contentious and non-contentious, and Mr. Wubben can subsequently make whatever submissions he likes. May I add one final matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: A large part of what Mr. Wubben is saying is based on his submission that there's no evidence that some of these signatures are non-contentious. We may yet have some evidence from this witness about that. But even -- even if we already had evidence in the form of an affidavit or a witness, the Prosecution would still be free to dispute that evidence, in which case it would still not be agreed that it's non-contentious and we would be back to square one. Frankly I'm allowed to use the terms contentious and non-contentious, because that's what's used in the expert's report, and Mr. Wubben is free to make submissions and cross-examine about whether they really are non-contentious in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think you haven't asked the witness to explain his choice of -- what does he mean by contentious and non-contentious. And of course we cannot ask you to put that question because that question can be put on cross-examination by Mr. Wubben himself. So that's the position. I mean, you have to concede that the choice of language has been not the Defence but the expert witness. He is the one who says N1 is -- or whatever is a non-contentious handwriting or a non-contentious signature. Of course you will ask him the question, and if you don't, probably we will ask him the question at the end. Because we want to know how he comes to the conclusion at least -- or comes to the conclusion before making his analysis that some documents are -- contain no contentious handwriting, some documents contain no contentious signatures. So you are free to ask him the question, but I cannot preclude the Defence from putting questions using those terms simply because it is the expert himself who is using those terms. Do you read me?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I read you. But I have an objection to make with respect to the qualification of non-contentious. Non-contentious --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, okay, but that becomes a submission later on. It's not even -- a non-contentious by party. It's the description that this expert is giving us. Now, later on you will be free to put to him any question you like and -- by way of trying to elicit an explanation from him why he chooses to consider N4 and N5 as containing no contentious handwriting and signature, for example. And if you're not happy with the reply that you will receive from him, then of course you're free to make submissions. And we will draw our conclusions as well later on as to whether we can really refer to these as non-contentious or contentious; it's important. I concede that the difference is of course important because if a handwriting or a signature is non-contentious, it means that it has not been contested, to me, in my simple English. We'll come to this later, but of course you will have every opportunity to put the question and to make submissions in regard, but I cannot stop the Defence from putting the question -- putting questions referring to the same terminology used by the expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will make that submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We will have 30 minutes starting from now, basically 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Professor Bilic, before the break we were starting to look at your report, and in particular the part where you refer to the samples of contentious and non-contentious documents. It might help to explain the meaning of non-contentious documents, as used in your report. Would it be correct to say that by "non-contentious" you mean those documents that you take to be authentic for the purposes of comparison and analysis?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let's, in fact, go through one by one the non-contentious samples, and in fact starting with that of Hamdija Fejzic first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's give it a number straight away. The number that it has in the report so that we can follow you without difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: An exhibit number for the report, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No -- my apologies. I misunderstood Your Honour. I thought Your Honour was about to assign an exhibit number for the whole report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I am not going to assign any numbers. We will keep -- otherwise because it will be confusion galore. You know, I mean, it will be Trial Chamber-promoted confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. I just mean an exhibit number for the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the report I think we can give it a number straight away, but I'm not going to be giving any other numbers to any other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, and we won't be tendering non-contentious documents. We don't propose to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's up to you. We told you last time that's not our business, it's yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, indeed. So I'm not sure what the next exhibit will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know what the next number -- 1011, 1012?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D1012, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: D1012. So Professor Bilic's report will become Defence Exhibit D1012. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And just for the record, the Prosecution contests the admittance of this report regarding the parts concentrating on the non-contentious documents and the qualification, as such, acceptance of the so-called K documents, partly attributed to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let's go through the non-contentious samples, and in fact I want to start with those of Hamdija Fejzic. So if you turn to page 4 of your report and you go down to paragraph 3 you see where it says original documents with non-contentious handwriting and signature by Hamdija Fejzic. And then we see N1, N2, N3, N4, N5? Now, did you in fact personally obtain what you call the non-contentious samples from Hamdija Fejzic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, in fact, did that occur? Did he come to your office or did you see him or what precisely?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to an agreement with the Defence, the gentleman called into the office of Madam Vasvija Vidovic and Mr. John Jones, and then we set up an appointment for him to come to my laboratory. He arrived and presented his uncontentious documents, which I have listed on pages 4 and 5. When he presented these documents, I asked Mr. Hamdija Fejzic to take a piece of paper with squares on it - it's very important to have that kind of paper - and to write something on it, a certain text, in handwriting, which he did. I also asked for a sample of his signature, and he signed his name in the standard, usual way he does so. Documents N1, 2, and 3 were official documents which had court stamps on them. They were certified documents. So these were indisputably his signatures over a certain time period. Mr. Hamdija Fejzic did not have any other samples from the period in question, which is quite logical since it was wartime, but he did provide signatures of a good enough quality and quantity to enable expert analysis and to make possible the reaching of a final conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now I want to go to what you described as non-contentious documents or non-contentious handwriting signatures of the late Hamed Salihovic. Now, as you said, he is in fact deceased. Did you request samples of non-contentious handwriting of this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: It took quite a long time and a lot of effort to find them, but finally we did in the archives of the facility of mathematics and science where the deceased had been a student. These documents are in the archives, where they are kept for a long time, so that in the file in the facility archives there was quite a lot of material, including signatures by him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, we'll pass up a new exhibit. It's not set out in any exhibit lists because it's arisen in light of the objections expressed by the Prosecution today, and I trust that in any event there will be plenty of time before cross-examination for that to be studied. And if that could be shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there might be some confidence in the time for preparing this as expressed by the Defence counsel. I haven't seen it. This is the first time. And I protest that it is even announced as being produced today at court. I think this is not the professional way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I might respond. It wasn't until today that we knew the Prosecution was contesting that these non-contentious documents by Hamed Salihovic were in fact non-contentious and that they had put us on notice that they required evidence in that regard. We've been put on notice. We're providing evidence in that regard, so I really don't see how my learned friend can object. If it's a matter of preparation, then of course if -- if he needs more time to study this document before he starts his cross-examination, that's one matter. But surely there can't be an objection in principle to tendering an exhibit of this nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In reply to the statement by my learned friend, first we challenged in our motion, 94 bis, the recourse. Second, non-contentious means non-contentious between parties, so Defence counsel should be aware that that label does not apply, as they never invited us for such an opinion. And last Wednesday my colleague, Ms. Patricia Sellers, in the -- in this court confirmed that non-contentious documents are only the documents agreed upon by parties. So from that time, that should be even more specific. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I'm sure that when you read this document, Mr. Wubben, you realise that you will have ample time to deal with it and put any questions that you might wish to in the course of the three/four days that the witness will be with us here. So for the time being we will admit this document, give it to a number, D1013. And all it states is that way back in 2003, before the case started, these two persons signed below gave the -- Madam Vidovic a folio -- the personal file of Hamed Salihovic for the purpose of graphological examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, have you seen this receipt before?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that -- was that the receipt which was attached to the Hamed Salihovic non-contentious documents?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, along with the entire file which was in a folder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now, if we turn to the non-contentious documents relating to Naser Oric, we see on page 4 you have N1, N2, N3, N4, and then N5 to N12. Now, leave N5 to N12 aside because that has an ERN number. Can you tell us how you came into possession of N1 to N4?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: I came into possession of this sample from Mrs. Vasvija Vidovic, who had prepared the documents beforehand. I received them personally from her. These are official documents, and they are listed under N1, N2, N3, whereas documents N5 to N12 are samples taken from one year and one point in time. Documents N1, N2, and N3 are official documents which are certified and which were created in 1969, 1999 -- 1996 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And 2001 and later and before, and these are all allegedly signed by Naser Oric. I took these documents with a reserve, but I did not attach the same weight to these as I did to N1, N2, and N3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, just for clarification, which documents did you attach reserve to? If that's not clear, I can put the question again. You said you had some reservations about some of these documents. Which ones, again for the record, which --

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had reservations in respect of the documents N5 to N12, and this was why somebody made a cardinal mistake, and that was that somebody asked that these suspect, contentious document be signed and dated at the top right corner. It was asked of Mr. Naser Oric to sign and place a date on these contentious documents. He could have been and should have been asked to do so on any other document but the document which is contested. The contentious documents which are subject of examination must not be written upon in -- by way of additions or signatures or dates. I have very rich experience in examining these documents, and I took them with a certain reservation. How can we examine a document in the light of whether it contains Naser Oric's signature or not if he has been asked to put his signature on the same document? It has some consequences, adverse consequences, for the subsequent examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, leaving N5 to N12 aside, N1, N2, N3, N4, did that provide a sample sufficient for analysis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which -- yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. I hate to interrupt, but a matter for clarification, my learned friends asked questions about the alleged non-contentious documents, and the expert -- he skipped number N4; he didn't clarify about N4. And he addressed also the year of 2001, and it appears not to be on the group as mentioned in page 4 of the report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And perhaps 1996 and -- you are right there. Let's take them --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think the last error got corrected, 1996, 1969. Certainly I can ask about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you better do, actually. And I'm not quite clear in my mind whether N4 has been included or not yet included in any of these two groups that the witness has referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness Bilic, what would you say about N4?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: N4 is -- was only examined for handwriting. It does not contain signatures. And since we were supposed to examine the signatures, I only included it here because I had received it from Madam Vasvija Vidovic. I described it as such, as containing non-contentious block capital handwriting. I could not use it for the purposes of examining his signature because it did not contain one. I merely elicit it here as one of the documents I had received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Let's turn to N1, N2, and N3, and I'll clarify the dates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: These documents 5 to 12, you told us that there is a signature put on by Naser Oric. Could you describe where this signature has been put -- on which -- if there have been two sides of the document and which side?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think these are available, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, it's P100.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These we had seen in the beginning of the trial and we can see them again. If we have indication of the exhibit number, we can see them now. They were --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If it helps, I can put an example on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you have at least one that we can see on the ELMO, it will sure -- I'm sure satisfy Judge Eser. I do remember vividly how they were, but it would help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'm putting N5, so that should -- should help clarify matters in that -- yes. The Professor is pointing to a signature at the top and the date is 23 May, 2001. That's the non-contentious signature. And then I think we will see that there are two ERN numbers on this document signifying -- yes. The one was the document's original ERN and then it was re-assigned a new ERN once it had been signed. And then there's another signature further down the document there, and that would be -- that would be a contentious signature, in our submission, and I can't recall whether it's a Q -- I think it's Q16, I believe -- no. I'm not sure. It's a Q as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Could we see the whole page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. We are not seeing the whole page. We have to go further up. There you see. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you so much, Mr. Jones. I recognise again Mr. Wubben. Yes, please, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: For your information, this is K1. So the whole range is K1 up to K8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We have actually already, one of my staff has actually grouped them together with particular reference to how they are referred to in one --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One recorded --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's also Q4 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't have it with me at the moment. I have to look it up in one of these documents. Well, actually I do have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A question for you, Professor Bilic. Just looking at N1, N2, and N3, was that a sufficient sample for analysis?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Relatively speaking, it was sufficient. Why? Because documents of official character had to be collected where a person was not writing on request but spontaneously. Like, for instance, receipt on -- of money or goods or a payment slip. Any document which a person must have signed personally. This goes to show, the character of a document, goes to show that the person had to sign it personally in order to make it valid, to make use of it. We can see which documents these were; they are contained here, whereas taking -- a deliberate taking of samples by asking a person to write on a contested document is not the way to be done. Therefore, examination can be carried out only if in addition to such on-request handwriting one also has pieces of spontaneous writing. This could have been solved by obtaining documents of such character which date from a certain, continuous period of time. One has to pay attention to the fact that these signatures come from a period of time, that they -- they were placed over a certain period of time. And this is the sort of documentation that we had here. I hope I've made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps one final clarification, and perhaps you can answer this shortly. In other words, if you had in regard to Naser Oric only N.5 to N.12, which you've spoken about, the signatures dated 23 May 2001, would that have been sufficient for your analysis?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC
utterances.text: Quite sufficient, because they were of sufficient quantity and quality. Had I needed any more copies, I would have sought them --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
